blocks.en: In a neutral atom the number of protons is the atomic number and the number of electrons is the same. The number of neutrons is the mass number minus the atomic number.

blocks.cap: Sodium: 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 11 electrons in the shells 2, 8, 1.
Carbon: 6 protons, 6 neutrons, 6 electrons in the shells 2, 4.
Oxygen: 8 protons, 8 neutrons, 8 electrons in the shells 2, 6.

blocks.en: How to make the model

items.en: Take a piece of cardboard or thermocol for each atom and draw circles for the shells with a compass: two circles for carbon and oxygen, three for sodium.
Make the nucleus in the middle from clay: one colour for the protons and another for the neutrons (sodium 11 and 12, carbon 6 and 6, oxygen 8 and 8).
Stick beads of a third colour on the circles for the electrons: sodium 2, 8 and 1; carbon 2 and 4; oxygen 2 and 6.
Write the name, the symbol and the numbers of protons, electrons and neutrons under each model, and add a key to the colours.

blocks.en: What to say when presenting

items.en: Every atom is neutral: the protons (positive) and the electrons (negative) are equal in number.
The mass of the atom sits in the nucleus, where the protons and neutrons are.
Sodium has one electron in its outer shell and loses it easily to form Na⁺; oxygen has six and gains two to form O²⁻; carbon has four and shares them.

blocks.en: Bohr's theory (1913): electrons move around the nucleus only in fixed circular paths called shells or energy levels (K, L, M, N). An electron in a shell does not lose energy; it jumps to a higher shell when it takes in energy and falls back when it gives energy out as light. The shell number n can hold at most 2n² electrons: 2, 8, 18, 32.

blocks.cap: Example model, chlorine-35: 17 protons and 18 neutrons in the nucleus; 17 electrons in the K, L and M shells (2, 8, 7).

items.en: Draw the nucleus in the middle and write the protons and neutrons in it.
Draw one circle for each shell and label them K, L, M outwards.
Put the electrons on the circles, filling K first (2), then L (8), then M.
Write the atomic number, the mass number and the electron arrangement under the model and display it in the laboratory.

blocks.en: 1. Radioactive tracers in medicine

A radioactive tracer is a small amount of a radioactive isotope that is swallowed, injected or breathed in. The radiation it gives out is picked up by a scanner outside the body, so doctors can see where the tracer goes and how an organ is working. Larger doses of some isotopes are used to destroy diseased cells.

rows: The most used tracer: scans of bones (fractures, spread of cancer), heart (blood flow), lungs and kidneys.
The thyroid takes up iodine, so it shows the size and working of the thyroid; a larger dose treats an overactive thyroid and thyroid cancer.
PET scans: it collects in cells that use a lot of sugar, so it shows cancers and active areas of the brain.
Not a tracer: its gamma rays are directed at a tumour from outside the body to treat cancer (radiotherapy).

blocks.en: These isotopes are safe in small amounts because most have short half-lives (technetium-99m about 6 hours, fluorine-18 about 2 hours, iodine-131 about 8 days), so the radiation soon dies away.
2. Models of Rutherford and Bohr (group work)

items.en: Rutherford model (1911): a tiny, dense, positive nucleus in the centre, with the electrons moving around it like planets round the sun; most of the atom is empty space. Make it from a clay ball for the nucleus, wire rings and beads for the electrons, without labelled shells.
Bohr model (1913): electrons only in fixed shells K, L, M with fixed energy. Make it with labelled rings and the number of electrons each ring can hold (2, 8, 18).
Share the work: group 1 makes the Rutherford model, groups 2 to 5 make Bohr models of hydrogen, carbon, sodium and chlorine.
When presenting, compare them: Rutherford's atom could not explain why the electrons do not spiral into the nucleus; Bohr's shells did, and also explained the colours of light given out by hydrogen.

blocks.cap: Bohr model of hydrogen: 1 proton, 1 electron.
Bohr model of carbon: 6 protons, 6 neutrons, shells 2, 4.

work.starts: evolution of the current periodic table

blocks.en: Mendeleev's table (1869) put the elements in order of atomic mass and left gaps for elements not yet found. After 1900 it became the table we use today:

rows: Discovered the noble gases (argon, helium on Earth, neon, krypton, xenon), which added a new group at the right of the table.
Proposed the long form of the table, with the transition elements between the groups: the layout in use today.

Showed by X-ray spectra that the atomic number (number of protons), not atomic mass, fixes the order of the elements: the modern periodic law. It cured the misplaced pairs (for example argon and potassium) and showed which elements were still missing.
His electron shells explained why elements of a group behave alike (same number of outer electrons) and why the periods end after 2, 8, 8 elements.
Made technetium, the first element produced artificially, filling the gap at atomic number 43.
Discovered plutonium and other elements after uranium and placed the actinides in a separate row below the table, like the lanthanides; Nobel Prize 1951.
Approved the names nihonium (113), moscovium (115), tennessine (117) and oganesson (118), completing the seventh period: 118 elements.

items.en: Before 1900: Döbereiner's triads (1829), Newlands' octaves (1864), Mendeleev and Meyer (1869).

blocks.en: Linus Pauling (1901 to 1994) was an American chemist, born in Portland, Oregon. He used quantum mechanics to explain how atoms bond.

rows: Paper on the nature of the chemical bond: the idea of hybrid orbitals (for example the four equal bonds of carbon) and of resonance.

Introduced the electronegativity scale (fluorine 4.0 is the highest). The difference in electronegativity tells how unequally two atoms share a pair: none gives a non-polar covalent bond, a small difference a polar covalent bond, a large difference an ionic bond.
Published the book The Nature of the Chemical Bond.
Showed sickle-cell anaemia is a disease of one changed molecule (haemoglobin) and found the shape of protein chains (the alpha helix).
Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his research into the nature of the chemical bond.
Nobel Peace Prize (presented in 1963) for his campaign against nuclear weapons tests.

blocks.en: His main point for this unit: a bond is not simply ionic or covalent; most bonds lie between the two, and electronegativity measures how far a bond is from the equal sharing of electrons.

items.en: What you see: the brown bromine vapour moves out of its jar into the jar of air above it, until both jars have the same brown colour.

Why: gas particles move all the time in every direction. Bromine particles spread out of the crowded jar into the jar that has none, and the air particles spread the other way, until they are evenly mixed. This spreading is called diffusion.
What it proves: gases mix on their own, without stirring. Bromine vapour is much heavier than air, yet it still goes upwards, so the mixing is caused by the motion of the particles, not by weight.
Care: bromine is poisonous and burns the skin; the teacher does this in a fume cupboard.
What you see: a few drops of liquid bromine at the bottom of a closed jar turn into brown vapour, which slowly rises and fills the jar until the colour is the same everywhere.

Why: the bromine particles leave the liquid, move about in the air and spread to the places where there are fewer of them. This is diffusion; it is slow because the particles keep hitting air particles.
Conclusion: diffusion takes place in gases, and also from a liquid into a gas; the particles of matter are always moving.
Care: only the teacher handles liquid bromine, in a fume cupboard.

blocks.en: A crystalline solid has its particles in a regular repeating pattern, a sharp melting point and flat faces. An amorphous solid has its particles in no regular pattern and softens over a range of temperature before it melts.

items.en: Molar mass of CuSO₄·5H₂O = 63.6 + 32 + (4 × 16) + (5 × 18) = 249.6 g per mol.
Mass needed for 1 dm³ of 0.5000 M solution = 0.5000 mol × 249.6 g per mol = 124.8 g.
Weigh 124.8 g of the blue crystals on a balance and dissolve them in some water.
Pour the solution into a 1.0 dm³ volumetric flask, rinsing the beaker into the flask so that no solute is lost.
Add water up to the neck of the flask, stopper it and shake; then fill carefully to the 1.0 dm³ mark, put the stopper back and turn the flask over at least 10 times to mix.
Check: 0.5000 mol in 1.000 dm³ = 0.5000 mol per dm³ = 0.5000 M.

blocks.en: Conclusion: like dissolves like. Salt is ionic and vinegar is polar, so both dissolve in polar water. Iodine is non-polar, so it hardly dissolves in polar water, but it dissolves in methylated spirit because the spirit's C₂H₅ part is non-polar.
